name: Matthias Mason & Co.'s Blacksmith Shop

documented_range.note: SELF-REPORTED IN THE CHICAGO DEMOCRAT, AND THE ADVERTISEMENT RAN FOR A YEAR. Mason & Co. advertise as blacksmiths in the issue of 26 November 1833, on 'Main-street, nearly opposite Graves' Tavern'. The '& Co.' says the shop employed more than one man. Eleven printings of that one notice are now read out of the Democrat, the last on 10 December 1834, all under the same copy date - so the firm is documented trading thirteen months and not one day, and the far end of the range is inferred from a shorter reach than it was: a working smithy in a town growing tenfold is far more likely to have continued than to have closed. THE NOTICE CHANGES ITS ANCHOR PART WAY THROUGH, and the position note is where that is set out.

change_note: The building as this dataset can state it on the scene date. Where the sources give a size, a plan or a fabric, the record carries it; where they do not, the note says so attribute by attribute.

placement.position_note: THE ADDRESS IS DOCUMENTED IN A STREET NAME NOBODY ELSE USES, AND THE CROSS-REFERENCE IS WHAT PLACES IT. 'Main-street' appears nowhere in data/traces/street_control.json, the Thompson plat module or either 1834 sheet. Graves' Tavern is Dexter Graves's log tavern, which this dataset models as mansion_house at what became 84-86 Lake Street, on the NORTH side of Lake near Dearborn. 'Nearly opposite' therefore puts the smithy on the SOUTH side of Lake Street facing north across it, and 'Main-street' in November 1833 is very probably Lake Street under a colloquial name. The northing is the Lake Street south frontage band this dataset's reconstruction recipes already use; the easting is set opposite mansion_house. WHAT IS INVENTED: the exact lot, the setback and the facade bearing. AND THE ADVERTISEMENT DOES NOT KEEP THIS ANCHOR. Seven printings to 11 June 1834 read 'nearly opposite Graves' Tavern'; from 10 September 1834 the same standing copy, word for word otherwise and under the same 26 November 1833 dateline, reads 'opposite the Tremont House' - four printings, the last on 10 December 1834. The Democrat carries no printing of it between those two dates, so the change is bracketed by 1834-06-11 and 1834-09-10 and no closer. The first Tremont House stands at the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn in this dataset, about 36 m west of mansion_house and on the same north side of the street, so the later reading would put this shop the same distance west along the same south frontage. NOTHING PRINTED SAYS WHICH CHANGED - the shop may have moved, or the house across from it may have changed hands and name, or a compositor may have been handed fresh copy for a reason nobody printed; all three read exactly like this. THE POSITION HERE IS THE EARLIER READING'S AND HAS NOT BEEN MOVED, because moving it would decide that question on no evidence. The scene date is 1835-07-01, ten months after the later reading first ran, and the dated history of both anchors is carried in data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json under business_matthias_mason_co.

footprint.note: PLACEHOLDER - NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED. 20 x 30 ft is a two-fire shop: room for two hearths, an anvil each and a horse standing in, which is what '& Co.' implies. Every number is invented.

occupants.note: Matthias Mason and at least one partner or journeyman - the firm advertises as 'Mason & Co.' (data/residents/households/hh_mason_matthias.json). No other name is given. The Democrat sets the style four ways across eleven printings of one notice - 'Matthias Mason & Co.', 'Matthias Mason & Co., blacksmiths', 'MA[T]HIAS MASON & CO.' where the impression drops a T, and 'MATTHIAS MA[SON & CO.]' where the line is damaged - and the newspaper gazetteer holds all four as one house under business_matthias_mason_co, with the reasoning written out in data/research/newspapers/identity.json.

persons.name: Matthias Mason
persons.note: HIS ADDRESS NAMES A STREET THIS PROJECT DOES NOT OTHERWISE HOLD. 'Main-street' appears nowhere in this dataset's street control, the Thompson plat module or either 1834 sheet, and it is a real 1833 Chicagoan's own word for where his shop was. The cross-reference is usable: Graves' Tavern is Dexter Graves's house, the log tavern on Lake Street that became the Mansion House at what are now 84-86 Lake Street. So 'Main-street' in November 1833 is very probably Lake Street or a stretch of it under a colloquial name. THAT IS A FINDING FOR THE STREETS LAYER, NOT A PLACEMENT, and it is recorded here rather than acted on. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds; an advertiser in it was paying to be found, which makes it strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835, nineteen months and about 2,400 people later. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Mason, Matthias” (poll_1834_070, line 239). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Mason' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

residents.research_note: THE ADVERTISEMENT THAT CONTAINS A STREET NAME NOBODY ELSE USES, which is the most useful thing in this household and has nothing to do with its people. A blacksmith is also the trade the inferred phase will need most of: a town of 3,265 with the wagon traffic Andreas describes could not run on the two smithies this dataset models, and this record is the documented proof of a third.
